summary:
Scope and limits. I re-read the abstract, the introduction contributions (manuscript_filled.md l.22-27), Sections 2, 4 and 6.3/6.5, Discussion 7.1, the Conclusion, the highlights and the cover letter against REVIEW/review_01.md and response_01.md. I searched the web for prior art on: Y-binned/label-conditional conformal regression, density-level scores with stratum-specific thresholds, size optimality under class- or stratum-specific coverage, floor-type dual guarantees, and label-shift robustness of Mondrian CP. Search was limited to the WebSearch tool. arxiv.org, cambridge.org and api.crossref.org were blocked by this session's network policy, so I could not read full texts. Claims about papers the manuscript does not yet cite rest on abstracts and search-engine excerpts, and the authors should check them against the full papers. I recomputed ablation ratios read-only from results/raw_eval_v3 and results/confirmatory/raw_eval_v3.

Overall verdict. The cycle-1 prior-art fixes are largely adequate:
- Stratified calibration is now credited as BCCP / Mondrian / BFQR.
- Theorem 1 is explicitly not claimed as new.
- Proposition 2 is framed as the per-stratum form of Lei et al. 2013, Sadinle et al. 2019 and Kiyani et al. 2024.
- Kandinsky CP is described correctly (label-dependent, overlapping and fractional groups; minimax-optimal high-probability bound; regression experiment).
- BFQR's level optimisation and its Theorem 4.1 are described correctly.
- Corollary 1 credits Podkopaev & Ramdas, Angelopoulos-Barber-Bates and Barber et al. 2023.
- The floor variant is disclaimed as a contribution.

I found no prior paper that already proposes conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds for regression together with the plug-in optimality result. That narrow combination survives. What survives is modest, however: the theory is a direct per-stratum transfer of known level-set and Neyman-Pearson results, and the empirical gain over the information-matched baseline is about 2%.

Remaining problems:
1. The headline compares SDLC against the default absolute-residual score of BCCP, not against BCCP as published and implemented. BCCP is score-agnostic, and its reference package offers a heteroscedastic score that the manuscript never mentions (C1-02 items 1 and 3 not done).
2. The method-specific ingredient of SDLC, the nonparametric noise density, is not supported on held-out data: SDLC vs SDLC-N = 0.986, 11/6 datasets, p = 0.22 in my recomputation. Yet the abstract and highlights say "SDLC gave the smallest stratum-valid sets ... confirmed on 17".
3. The "coverage reallocation" result is presented as a contribution without crediting the known null-region / single-threshold behaviour of density level sets. The Sadinle null-region discussion promised under C1-04 is absent.
4. Two 2025-2026 papers are uncited although they bear on Proposition 2 and on the floor variant: Ding, Fermanian & Salmon (ICLR 2026) and Bhattacharyya, Ding & Barber (arXiv:2606.28598).
5. The abstract and Highlights 2-3 present the established stratified-calibration guarantee and an oracle result without attribution or qualification.

Every fix is text or a re-analysis of existing files; no new experiment is required.

issues.title: Headline 'SDLC vs bin-conditional conformal prediction' compares against BCCP's default score only; BCCP's own heteroscedastic score and reference package are not acknowledged (C1-02 fix inadequate)
issues.evidence:
Cycle 1 asked (REVIEW/review_01.md C1-02, actions 1, 3 and 7a) to rename the comparison 'BCCP with the absolute-residual score' and to say that BCCP is score-agnostic and that its reference implementation offers a heteroscedastic score. response_01.md C1-42 says 'pintervals ... added (all verified)'.

The manuscript does not do this:
- The bib key randahl2026pintervals is never cited. grep over manuscript/ and the supplement finds no 'pintervals' and no 'heterogeneous'.
- The abstract (l.8) still says 'smaller than bin-conditional conformal prediction on 24 of 31 datasets'.
- Sec. 5.4 (l.214) defines BCCP as 'the absolute-residual score with stratum-wise thresholds'.
- Highlight 4 and Conclusion l.511 repeat the framing.

The CRAN documentation of pinterval_bccp lists ncs_type options absolute_error, relative_error, za_relative_error, heterogeneous_error and raw_error. heterogeneous_error is |y - yhat| divided by a linear-model fit of |error| on yhat (rdrr.io/cran/pintervals). The package also has a companion paper: Randahl, Hjort & Williams, arXiv:2601.03994 (Jan 2026).

S-NCP is therefore BCCP with a stronger version of BCCP's own heteroscedastic option. By the manuscript's own decomposition, most of the 'gain over BCCP' is that option, not SDLC:
- CTR23 (Table 5): S-NCP vs BCCP = 0.926, p = 0.111.
- Held-out data, my recomputation (geometric mean of per-dataset mean-size ratios, alpha = 0.1, S5): S-Res vs S-NCP = 0.882, 12/5 datasets, Wilcoxon p = 0.03.
- The novelty-relevant comparison is SDLC vs S-NCP: 0.975 [0.941, 1.020] on CTR23 and 0.977 [0.940, 1.028] on held-out data.
issues.corrective_action:
1. Name the baseline 'BCCP (absolute-residual score)' everywhere: abstract, Highlight 4, Sec. 5.4, Tables 2/5/7, Conclusion and cover letter.
2. In Sec. 2.2 and Sec. 5.4, add one sentence: BCCP is score-agnostic, and its reference implementation (pintervals; cite randahl2026pintervals and arXiv:2601.03994) offers a heteroscedastic score |y - yhat| / sigma(yhat), of which S-NCP is a cross-fitted, covariate-based version.
3. Rewrite the abstract's size sentence so the primary efficiency claim is against S-NCP (ratios 0.975 / 0.977, with CIs including 1, and win counts). Mention BCCP with the residual score only secondarily.
4. Optional, from cache: evaluate pintervals' exact heterogeneous_error score (sigma linear in yhat, fitted on training residuals) as 'BCCP-het' on the 31 + 17 datasets at alpha = 0.1. This closes the original C1-02(7a) request.
issues.new_experiment: Optional: BCCP-het = stratified calibration with score |y - mu_hat(x)| / (a + b * mu_hat(x)), where a and b come from OLS of the absolute out-of-fold training residuals on mu_hat. Evaluate from the cached model outputs on 31 CTR23 x 10 seeds and 17 held-out x 5 seeds at alpha = 0.1, S5. Report SDLC/BCCP-het and S-NCP/BCCP-het geometric-mean ratios with bootstrap CIs and Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p.

issues.title: The method-specific component of SDLC (nonparametric noise density) is not confirmed on held-out data, yet SDLC is claimed to give 'the smallest stratum-valid sets ... confirmed on 17'
issues.evidence:
Contribution 2 (l.25) and Sec. 4.3 present SDLC's distinctive ingredient as the semiparametric density, whose noise law is a cross-fitted KDE plus a t2 defensive mixture. The ablation SDLC-N replaces it with a Gaussian.

CTR23 (Table 5): SDLC vs SDLC-N = 0.993 [0.985, 0.999], 23/8, Holm p = 0.068.

On the 17 held-out datasets, SDLC-N was evaluated (it is present in results/confirmatory/raw_eval_v3/*.jsonl) but is not reported and was not in C-H3 (PREREGISTRATION_confirmatory.md l.43). My recomputation (read-only Python over those files; per-dataset mean 'size' at alpha = 0.1, scheme S5, cal_frac 1; geometric mean of ratios; scipy Wilcoxon):
- SDLC vs SDLC-N: 0.986, 11/6, p = 0.22.
- SDLC-N vs S-NCP: 0.992, 14/3, p = 0.008.
- SDLC vs S-HPD: 0.984, 15/2, p = 0.005, matching Table 7.
My unfiltered CTR23 recomputation gives SDLC vs SDLC-N = 0.993, 23/8, raw p = 0.036, consistent with the paper's Holm value.

On held-out data the simpler Gaussian-density score therefore does as well as SDLC. The 'confirmed' advantage belongs to the density weighting 1/sigma(x), not to the estimator that defines SDLC. This contradicts:
- Highlight 4: 'SDLC gave the smallest stratum-valid sets on 31 datasets, confirmed on 17'.
- The abstract: 'SDLC gave the smallest stratum-valid sets'.
- 'SDLC (blue) does so with the smallest sets' (Fig. 2 caption).
The Gaussian level-set score -phi(z)/sigma(x) is itself a simple transformation of the normalised residual (|z| <= sqrt(2(c - log sigma(x)))), which makes the methodological novelty of SDLC beyond 'use a density score in BCCP' thin.
issues.corrective_action:
1. Report SDLC vs SDLC-N on the held-out datasets in Sec. 6.5 or Supplementary S6, explicitly labelled as not pre-registered.
2. Reword the abstract, Highlight 4, the Fig. 2 caption and Conclusion l.511. Example: 'density-level scores (SDLC and its Gaussian version SDLC-N) gave the smallest stratum-valid sets among the scores compared; the gain over a stratified normalised residual is about 2% and comes from the 1/sigma(x) weighting; the nonparametric noise shape added at most about 1% and was not significant on held-out data.'
3. In contribution 2, present the KDE noise model as an implementation choice, not as the source of the efficiency gain.
4. In Sec. 7.2, recommend SDLC-N or S-NCP as defaults when simplicity matters.
issues.new_experiment: None. Re-analysis of existing confirmatory raw files (SDLC-LS vs SDLC-N, Wilcoxon, sign test, bootstrap CI of the geometric-mean ratio), labelled exploratory.

issues.title: 'Coverage reallocation' is presented as a new result without crediting the known null-region / single-threshold behaviour of density level sets; promised Sadinle null-region discussion missing (C1-04 item 5)
issues.evidence:
The abstract (l.8) and contribution 1 (l.24) present 'we show that ... the gain over a normalised residual comes from reallocating coverage across inputs' as a theoretical contribution. The Sec. 4.2 remark (l.152) derives that in a location-scale model the optimal set is {u: g(u) >= t_k sigma(x)} and is empty when t_k sigma(x) > max g. It cites nothing.

This is the standard behaviour of a globally thresholded density level set:
- Sadinle, Lei & Wasserman (2019) analyse exactly these empty 'null regions' of least-ambiguous class-specific classifiers and propose remedies.
- Lei & Wasserman (2014) and Izbicki et al. (2020, 2022) motivate local bands, CD-split and HPD-split precisely because a single threshold on f(y|x) does not equalise conditional coverage across x.

REVIEW/review_01.md C1-04 action 5 asked the authors to 'discuss Sadinle et al.'s null-region remedies'. grep finds no 'null region' or 'ambigu' text in the manuscript or the supplement.
issues.corrective_action:
1. In the Sec. 4.2 remark, add: 'This is the location-scale form of the familiar behaviour of globally thresholded density level sets, which leave low-density inputs with small or empty sets (the null region of Sadinle et al., 2019; see also Lei & Wasserman, 2014; Izbicki et al., 2022); our addition is the explicit decomposition of the gain over S-NCP into the factor 1/sigma(x).'
2. Briefly mention Sadinle et al.'s remedies for empty sets (e.g. reporting a non-empty fallback) as an option for SDLC.
3. In the abstract and contribution 1, call this an 'explanation' rather than a separate result.

issues.title: Uncited 2025-2026 prior art on size-optimal sets under class-wise / macro coverage and on interpolating marginal and class-conditional thresholds (relevant to Proposition 2, the price analysis and SDLC-floor)
issues.evidence:
Two recent papers are not in references_verified.bib (grep for 'macro', 'Fermanian', 'Bhattacharyya' returns nothing relevant):

(a) Ding, Fermanian & Salmon, 'Conformal Prediction for Long-Tailed Classification', ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2507.06867). According to its abstract and v1 text, it derives the oracle prediction set that optimally trades off set size and macro-coverage (the average of class-conditional coverages). It also proposes a label-weighted method that interpolates the marginal and class-conditional conformal thresholds.

(b) Bhattacharyya, Ding & Barber, 'Conformal Prediction with Macro-Coverage Guarantees' (arXiv:2606.28598, June 2026). According to its abstract, it characterises the smallest prediction sets that satisfy generalised macro-coverage objectives, of which class-wise coverage is a special case, and gives a matching conformal score with finite-sample guarantees.

These are the classification precedents closest to Proposition 2 (size-optimal sets under label-indexed coverage constraints). They are also the closest precedents to:
- the 'price of stratum-wise validity' remark (l.150);
- SDLC-floor (l.182), which mixes a marginal and a stratified threshold to obtain dual guarantees and which the practical guidance recommends for small calibration sets (l.489).
Sec. 2.2 and Sec. 4.5 cite only Sadinle, Lei 2014, Kiyani, Wang et al. and Ding et al. 2023 (clustered CP). A related grouped extension, 'Macro Mondrian Conformal Risk Control' (arXiv:2610.35035), surfaced in search; I could not verify its content.
issues.corrective_action:
1. After reading the full texts, add (a) and (b) to Sec. 2.2 and to the sentence before Proposition 2: 'in classification, size-optimal sets under class-wise and macro-coverage constraints are characterised by Sadinle et al. (2019) and Bhattacharyya et al. (2026)'.
2. In Sec. 4.5, cite Ding, Fermanian & Salmon (2026) next to the floor variant as a principled way to interpolate between marginal and label-conditional thresholds.
3. Note in Sec. 7.3 that macro-coverage, an average over strata, is a weaker alternative target that could reduce the price reported in Table 3 when per-stratum guarantees are not required.
4. Verify all entries as for the rest of the bibliography.

issues.title: Abstract and highlights present established or oracle results without attribution or qualification
issues.evidence:
Abstract (l.8): 'Calibrating conformal thresholds within target strata guarantees stratum-wise coverage for any score' appears with no indication that this is BCCP / Mondrian prior art. A reader of the abstract alone will take it as a finding. The introduction (l.22) and cover letter are explicit about this; the abstract is not.

Highlight 2: 'Calibrating within target strata guarantees coverage of rare, extreme outcomes'. This lists a known property as a highlight of the paper. It also overstates the guarantee: the guarantee covers only the calibrated strata, and the uncalibrated top 1% was covered at 0.736 by SDLC (Table 2).

Highlight 3: 'Stratum-wise density level sets are the smallest stratum-valid prediction sets'. This omits that it is an oracle statement (Proposition 2) and the per-stratum form of known level-set results, as the text itself says at l.24 and l.134.

The abstract is exactly 250 words (the ESWA limit), so additions need compensating cuts.
issues.corrective_action:
1. Abstract: change to 'Calibrating thresholds within target strata, an established Mondrian device (bin-conditional conformal prediction), guarantees ...' and 'We show that oracle conditional-density level sets with stratum-specific thresholds, the per-stratum analogue of known level-set results, are the smallest ...'. Trim elsewhere, for example the decision-study sentence, to stay at or under 250 words.
2. Highlight 2: 'Established stratified calibration restores coverage of the calibrated tail strata'. Or replace it with a genuine finding, e.g. 'Lowering alpha is a less efficient way to protect tails than stratifying'.
3. Highlight 3: 'Oracle density level sets with stratum thresholds minimise stratum-valid set size'. Keep it at 85 characters or fewer.

issues.title: Proposition 3 credit omits the classification plug-in precedent; 'linear cost' is not a distinguishing contribution
issues.evidence:
l.140 says the proof of Proposition 3 'follows the plug-in arguments of Lei et al. (2013) and Izbicki et al. (2022)'. Sadinle et al. (2019), already cited for Proposition 2, also study plug-in estimation of the class-specific least-ambiguous classifier, which is the direct discrete analogue of Proposition 3. Their exact theorem numbers should be checked in the full text, which I could not access.

Proposition 3 gives only consistency, without rates, under sup-norm consistency of f_hat. The location-scale estimator satisfies this only under the correct model (l.164).

Contribution 2 (l.25) highlights 'an exact, stratum-exact implementation whose cost is linear in the number of test points'. Every split-conformal method is linear in the number of test points. The real difference is exactness relative to BCCP's grid over candidate outcomes.
issues.corrective_action:
1. Add Sadinle et al. (2019) to the credit sentence for Proposition 3, citing the relevant section after checking it.
2. State that Proposition 3 is a consistency result without rates.
3. Rephrase the implementation claim as 'exact set geometry without a grid over candidate outcomes (unlike grid-based BCCP), at O(G log K) per test point'.

issues.title: Duplicated and partly inconsistent description of BFQR in Sec. 2.2
issues.evidence: manuscript_filled.md l.50 introduces BFQR twice in consecutive sentences. First: 'their binned fair quantile regression (BFQR) splits Y into equal-mass bins and calibrates within each combination of group and bin, with a conformal step that maintains coverage'. Second: 'Their binned fair quantile regression (BFQR) forms equal-mass bins of the calibration outcomes ... chooses the bin levels beta_m ...'. The first version omits the level optimisation that the second (correct) version describes. This duplication was introduced by the C1-16 rewrite.
issues.corrective_action: Delete the first BFQR sentence in 015_related.md and keep the second, accurate description (equal-mass calibration bins, per-(group, bin) beta_m-quantiles of CQR scores, beta_m optimised subject to mean beta_m = 1 - alpha, Thm 4.1 bounds).
